channel.title: Field Notes
channel.description: Short, occasional essays on ideas worth sitting with.

item.title: The First Rule of Wealth Nobody Leads With
item.description: Before allocation, before compounding, before any of it — the actual first move, and why it's boring on purpose.
item.content:encoded:
Every wealth guide leads with the exciting part: index funds, compounding, asset allocation, the chart that goes up and to the right. Almost none of them lead with the part that actually determines whether you get to use any of it.

The first rule is this: know your number before you know your strategy. Not your net worth number — your burn number. What it actually costs you, per month, to live the life you already have. Most people can't answer this within twenty percent. That's not a knowledge problem, it's an avoidance problem, and it's the single biggest predictor of whether the rest of the advice ever gets applied.

Once you have that number, everything downstream gets simpler:

  1. You know exactly how much of a bad month you can absorb before it becomes a bad year.
  2. You know what "enough" would even look like, instead of chasing a moving target.
  3. You stop optimizing a portfolio you haven't actually earned the right to worry about yet.

None of this is clever. It's a spreadsheet and an evening. That's exactly why it gets skipped — it doesn't feel like progress, it just is progress.

item.title: A Note on This Design
item.description: Why the homepage is off-center, why it's this particular green, and why that's the point.
item.content:encoded:
The layout on this site is deliberately asymmetrical. The headline doesn't sit in the center of the page — it's pushed to one side, anchored to a grid, with a single graphic mark placed against it like a counterweight. Nothing here is centered because centered is the default, and the default doesn't ask you to look twice.

This is an old idea. Swiss graphic designers in the mid-twentieth century built entire systems around it: a strict underlying grid, used not to constrain expression but to make asymmetry legible rather than arbitrary. Off-center, but not random — every position on this page answers to the same twelve-column structure.

The type is a neo-grotesque sans for anything structural — titles, navigation, dates — because that family of typeface (Helvetica and its relatives) was built to disappear and let the hierarchy do the talking. The body text you're reading now is a serif instead, chosen for long-form reading rather than signage. Two jobs, two typefaces.

And the color: one solid, saturated, slightly uncomfortable green. Not decoration — contrast. Stark black text on a field that vibrates a little at the edges of your vision. It's meant to be seen once and remembered, the way a good cover should be.

None of this is subtle. That's also the point.

item.title: The Film That Recalibrated My Clock
item.description: A quiet drama about someone who ran out of time to be ordinary in, and what it changed about how I schedule mine.
item.content:encoded:
There's a scene, about two-thirds through, where the main character does nothing for four full minutes. No dialogue, no score, just a person sitting with a decision they already know they've made. Most films would have cut it down to fifteen seconds. This one trusts you to sit in it.

That's the whole argument of the movie, really: most of what matters happens in the parts we're trained to skip.

I walked out and canceled two meetings I didn't need to be in.

Worth watching for:

  • The four-minute scene, obviously
  • A supporting performance that says more with posture than the leads say with lines
  • An ending that refuses to resolve the one thing you want resolved

Not worth watching if you need plot momentum every ten minutes. This isn't that kind of film, and it isn't trying to be.

item.title: On Writing in Public
item.description: The first draft is never for anyone else. The second one might be.
item.content:encoded:
Most advice about writing online skips the part that actually matters: the first draft is not for your reader. It's for you, working out what you think by watching yourself say it.

The mistake is publishing that draft. The second mistake is never writing it at all, because you were waiting to already know what you meant.

A method that works, roughly:

  1. Write the bad version fast, with no audience in mind.
  2. Leave it alone for a day.
  3. Come back and cut everything that was you finding the idea, not stating it.

What's left is usually short. That's fine. Short and clear beats long and impressive almost every time, and it's much closer to the truth of what you actually think.

Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication — but only after you've earned it by going through the complicated version first.

Nobody skips the complicated version. They just don't publish it.

item.title: Welcome to Field Notes
item.description: Why this exists, what to expect, and why there's no algorithm deciding what you see.
item.content:encoded:
This is a newsletter in the oldest sense of the word: things worth noting, sent directly, on no schedule but the one dictated by having something to say.

There's no algorithm here. No engagement loop, no infinite scroll, no notification badge. If you want to keep reading, you subscribe to the RSS feed or you don't. That's the whole mechanism.

A few things you can expect:

  • Short essays, rarely more than a few hundred words
  • No paywall, no tiers, no upsell
  • Publishing when there's something worth publishing, not on a content calendar

If that sounds like your kind of thing, welcome. If not — no hard feelings, and thanks for stopping by.
